clue.text: American broadcast: professional golf and stuff

parts.note: a pro is a professional
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to ram is to stuff or cram

explanation.surface: A US sports broadcast covering professional golf and assorted other material.
explanation.walkthrough: PROGRAM is the American spelling; British English writes programme for a broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: A program is a single show on radio or television, spelt the US way without the final -me.

clue.text: Have gangs succeeded?

parts.note: posses are groups or gangs, originally of men summoned by a sheriff
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees

explanation.surface: A question asking whether gangs have been successful.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess is to own or hold something.

clue.text: Oscar exercises with judge after work

parts.note: O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet
PE is physical education, school exercises
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: Oscar does physical exercise with a judge after a day at work.
explanation.definitionFit: To operate is to function or run, as a machine works.

clue.text: Animal horn I carved

indicators.note: carved means cut into a new shape, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: An animal horn that someone has carved.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the animal is prized and poached for its horn.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhinoceros is a large thick-skinned mammal with one or two horns on its snout.

clue.text: Fish in sea spread

indicators.note: in places the fish inside the word for sea

parts.note: marine means of the sea
a gar is a long-snouted fish

explanation.surface: A fish found in the sea is spread out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for something spread on bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Margarine is a butter substitute that people put on toast and bread.

clue.text: Perceive intelligence shown by head

parts.note: wit is mental sharpness or intelligence
a ness is a headland, a head jutting into the sea, as in Loch Ness's neighbour place names

explanation.surface: Someone sees how clever the head of a school or firm is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' reads as a person in charge, but here it is the geographical head, a promontory, which is NESS in many British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: To witness something is to see it happen, so it works as a verb meaning observe or perceive.

clue.text: Start of week as the husband's taken out rubbish

indicators.note: start of means the first letter of week
taken out says a letter is removed from the word the

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: At the start of the week, the husband takes out the bins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken out rubbish' reads as a chore, but 'taken out' removes H from THE and 'rubbish' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste is unwanted material thrown away, the same as refuse.

clue.text: The large suspect holding piano wire

indicators.note: holding means the jumble contains the letter for piano
suspect as an adjective means dodgy, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly

explanation.surface: A large suspect has a length of piano wire, a classic murder weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: A wire was an old word for a telegram, and to wire meant to telegraph.
explanation.definitionFit: To wire someone is to send them a message by telegram, so wire and telegraph are synonyms.

clue.text: Obvious I had to enter competition

indicators.note: to enter means to go inside, so the contraction goes inside the word for competition

parts.note: an event is a sporting competition
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone says it was clear they had to enter the contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident means plain or clear to see.

clue.text: Second egg on tray — not oddly something one gets in hospital?

parts.note: to urge is to egg on or encourage

indicators.note: not oddly means skipping the odd letters, keeping the even ones of tray

explanation.surface: A hospital patient gets a second egg on the breakfast tray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'egg' reads as food on a hospital tray, but 'egg on' is a phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Patients in hospital may undergo an operation, which is the work of a surgeon.

clue.text: We desire pants wife's taken off, getting more sleazy

indicators.note: pants as a verb is slang for messes up or makes a mess of, so the letters are jumbled
taken off says the letter for wife is removed from the jumble

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A saucy scene: someone wants underwear the wife has removed, which is getting rather sleazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear but signals the anagram; WE DESIRE less W leaves EDESIRE, which rearranges to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedier is the comparative of seedy, which means disreputable or squalid in a sordid way.

clue.text: Current inside fuse is regular?

indicators.note: inside puts the current symbol within the word for fuse

parts.note: to solder is to fuse metal parts together
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An electrician wonders whether the current through a fuse is steady.
explanation.walkthrough: A regular, as a noun, is a professional soldier in a standing army rather than a reservist.
explanation.definitionFit: Regulars are full-time members of an army, so one regular is a professional serviceman.

clue.text: Cast are able to add more information

indicators.note: cast as in casting metal into a new shape, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: A theatre cast is capable of contributing extra details to the story.
explanation.definitionFit: To elaborate is to expand on something by giving further detail.

clue.text: Over in estate see game birds

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the run of words estate see game

parts.note: the letters run across the end of estate, all of see and the start of game

explanation.surface: On a country estate, someone spots game birds flying overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game birds' looks like the definition, but 'game' supplies the G and only 'birds' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Geese are large waterfowl, plural of goose, a kind of bird.

clue.text: Search could make son cry

parts.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
to weep is to cry

explanation.surface: A search for a lost child could reduce a son to tears.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweep is a thorough search of an area, as in a police sweep.

clue.text: Headteacher called out rule

indicators.note: called out means spoken, so the word sounds like the one for a headteacher

parts.note: a principal is the head of a school or college

explanation.surface: A headteacher shouts out a school rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A principle is a fundamental law or tenet that governs conduct.

clue.text: Inn with salty nuts — tons swallowed at once

indicators.note: swallowed says the letter for tons is taken inside the jumble
nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

explanation.surface: A pub serving salty nuts that get eaten by the ton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' looks like the bar snacks of the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Instantly means immediately, without any delay.

clue.text: Met this writer tucking into feasts I'd prepared

indicators.note: tucking into means slipping inside, so the setter's letter goes into the jumble
prepared means made ready, as a dish is, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: this writer is the setter, I

explanation.surface: A writer joins the feasts they had prepared and tucks in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' looks like eating, but it is a container signal; the writer of the clue is the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Demands or needs that are met have been fulfilled, as a condition is satisfied.

clue.text: Happy to tour in Africa?

indicators.note: to tour is to go around, so the word for happy goes around the word in

parts.note: content means happy or satisfied

explanation.surface: Someone is pleased to go on a trip in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows Africa is an example of the answer, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Africa is one of the large landmasses of the world, an instance of the general category.

clue.text: Children maintained no uniform is demanded

indicators.note: no means without, so the letter for uniform is taken out

parts.note: argued means maintained or asserted
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Children insisted there should be no school uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge a price is to ask or demand payment of it.

clue.text: Object after old knight pulled up zip

indicators.note: after puts the word for object after the reversed pair
pulled up in a down clue means read from bottom to top, reversing the letters

parts.note: N is the chess notation for knight
a thing is an object

explanation.surface: An item after an old knight's armour was pulled up by its zip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'zip' looks like a fastener, but in informal English it means zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is slang for nil or zero, the same as nought.

clue.text: Because of that layer, cake is hollow

parts.note: a layer is something that lays eggs, a hen

indicators.note: hollow means emptied of its middle, leaving just the first and last letters of cake

explanation.surface: A baker blames a particular layer for the cake coming out hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'layer' suggests a layer of cake, but it is a creature that lays, a hen.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence is an adverb meaning for this reason or as a consequence.

clue.text: More inquisitive about centre of Halifax getting louder

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for more inquisitive goes round the middle letter

parts.note: nosier is the comparative of nosy, prying

indicators.note: centre of means the middle letter of Halifax

explanation.surface: Someone is getting nosier about what goes on in the middle of Halifax, a Yorkshire town.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisier is the comparative of noisy, making more sound.

clue.text: Employs English errand boys? Not at first

indicators.note: not at first means losing the opening letter of the word for errand boys

parts.note: pages are boys employed to run errands

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether English errand boys were not hired at the outset.
explanation.definitionFit: To engage someone is to hire or take them on, so engages means employs.

clue.text: Somewhat important I catch lark

indicators.note: Somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it rather important to catch a songbird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lark' reads as the bird, but here it means a playful prank.
explanation.definitionFit: An antic is a piece of foolish or playful behaviour, much like a lark or caper.

clue.text: Watching old boy performing functions

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
serving is fulfilling a function or role

explanation.surface: A former pupil watches staff perform their duties.
explanation.definitionFit: Observing means watching attentively or noticing.

clue.text: Lays bare — writer's got nothing on

indicators.note: on in a down clue puts the letter for nothing on top of the rest

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing
pens are writers' tools; the possessive gives PEN plus S

explanation.surface: A writer has stripped naked and is wearing nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got nothing on' paints a naked writer, which fits 'Lays bare'; but 'on' just places O above PENS.
explanation.definitionFit: To open something up is to expose or reveal it to view.

clue.text: Ancestors tense wearing little jumpers

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so the jumpers contain the letter for tense

parts.note: roos is short for kangaroos, which jump
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Nervous ancestors dressed in small sweaters, a jumper being a British pullover.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British word for a sweater, but here the jumpers are kangaroos, shortened to roos.
explanation.definitionFit: Your roots are your family origins or forebears, the people you descend from.

clue.text: Clock spring ultimately slack and set to lose time

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, picking the final letter of spring

parts.note: limp means slack or floppy

indicators.note: to lose says a letter is taken away from the word set

explanation.surface: A clock's mainspring has gone slack and is set to lose time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clock' is the noun on the surface, but as a verb in slang it means to notice or catch sight of.
explanation.definitionFit: To clock someone is informal for spotting them, so a brief sighting fits the verb.

clue.text: Decreasing metal in goldfield, initially

parts.note: iron is a metal

indicators.note: initially means at the start, picking the first letter of goldfield

explanation.surface: Mining output of a metal in a goldfield is falling off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decreasing' reads as getting smaller, but split as de-creasing it means removing creases.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing clothes with a hot iron takes the creases out of them, a punning sense of the word.

clue.text: What students want? Flipping good education and freebees on a regular basis

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the letters for good and education are reversed
on a regular basis means taking every other letter of freebees

explanation.surface: Students supposedly want good teaching and lots of free gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive, but it signals reversal of G and ED to DEG.
explanation.definitionFit: University students study to earn qualifications, which are academic awards from a university.

clue.text: Heartlessly crumble, say, small leaves

indicators.note: heartlessly means losing the heart, the central letter of the word for a pudding, with the letter for small then added at the end

parts.note: a crumble is a kind of pudding, hence an example of a dessert

explanation.surface: Someone cruelly crushes small leaves, perhaps in a kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: A crumble is a British baked pudding of fruit under a crumbly topping. 'Heartlessly' drops the middle S of DESSERT and 'small' adds an S at the end, so in effect that S moves to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To desert someone is to abandon them, so the verb means leaves or walks out on.
